extra.message: SQL Injection in /users user lookup via id parameter — Full database compromise: extract all user credentials (plaintext passwords), PII, and active session tokens; modify or delete any database record. [verified: The `id` query parameter from line 36 is concatenated directly into `cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE id=" + id)` on line 39 with no parameterization, escaping, or validation; no middleware or decorator intercepts this path.]

OS Command Injection in /diag via domain parameter — Remote code execution on the server: arbitrary shell commands run as the web server process, full system compromise. [verified: The `domain` parameter (line 162) is passed to `subprocess.check_output(..., shell=True)` on line 163 with no sanitization; the `risk < 3` gate is a configuration toggle, not an input control, and the path is reachable when risk >= 3.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads in /extract — Remote code execution on the server: attacker can craft a pickle payload to execute arbitrary Python code and shell commands. [verified: The `object` query parameter is base64-decoded and passed to `pickle.loads()` on line 197 with no validation; the `risk < 3` check does not neutralize the vulnerability, and the code itself demonstrates an RCE payload via `__reduce__`.]

SQL Injection in /login via password parameter — Authentication bypass: login as any user (including admin) without knowing the password; extract all user credentials from the database. [verified: The `password` parameter on line 282 is concatenated unsanitized into SQL on line 288 (`AND password='" + password + "'`); only `username` is sanitized via `re.sub(r"[^\w]", '', ...)`, leaving the password field fully injectable.]

OS Command Injection via do_BDR HTTP Method Handler — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the DSVPWA process, enabling full system compromise. [verified: do_BDR passes self.path[1:] (the HTTP request path stripped of leading '/') directly to subprocess.check_output with shell=True; the only guard is risk<3 which is a configuration toggle, not a security control — an attacker sending 'BDR /;id; HTTP/1.1' achieves RCE when risk>=3.]

Weak SSL/TLS Configuration - SSLv3 Enabled, Compression Allowed, No Cipher Preference — TLS connections are vulnerable to POODLE (SSLv3), CRIME (compression), and cipher downgrade attacks, allowing decryption of supposedly secure traffic. [verified: Lines 39-41 explicitly clear OP_NO_SSLv3 (allowing POODLE-vulnerable SSLv3), OP_NO_COMPRESSION (enabling CRIME-vulnerable TLS compression), and OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE (ceding cipher selection to the client for downgrade attacks). All three insecure options are actively enabled on the reachable --ssl code path with no compensating control; this is a genuine weak-TLS configuration, not cosmetic]

Reflected Cross-Site Scripting in /post via msg parameter — Execute arbitrary JavaScript in victims' browsers: session theft via cookie exfiltration, credential phishing, DOM manipulation, redirection to malicious sites. [verified: The `msg` parameter (line 69) is returned as raw HTML content on line 75 via Python `.format()` with no HTML encoding; the CSP header `default-src * 'unsafe-inline'` explicitly permits inline scripts, providing no defense.]

Stored Cross-Site Scripting in /guestbook comment display — Persistent JavaScript execution for all visitors to the guestbook page: mass session hijacking, defacement, drive-by malware distribution. [verified: Stored comments are rendered on line 93 via `{}.format(column)` with no HTML escaping; the column values originate from user-supplied `comment` parameter (line 87) and flow through the database to output unencoded.]

Missing Authorization on /admin - only checks cookie existence — Unauthenticated access to administrative interface: any user with any session cookie can view admin pages and links. [verified: ExecutionAfterRedirect.run() only checks cookie existence (`if not cookie` on line 142) but never validates that the session maps to an authenticated user; any visitor who first hits `/login` (which sets a SESSIONID cookie per do_GET line ~178) can then access `/admin`.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read in /docs via path parameter — Read arbitrary files from the server filesystem: source code, configuration files, SSL private key (ssl/key.pem), /etc/passwd, database files. [verified: The `path` parameter (line 209) is passed to `open(os.path.abspath(path), 'rb')` on line 211 with no path restriction; `os.path.abspath` resolves but does not prevent traversal, and no allowlist or sandbox is applied.]

Server-Side Request Forgery in /docs via path parameter with URL scheme — Access internal network services and cloud metadata endpoints; scan internal infrastructure; exfiltrate data from internal services. [verified: When `path` contains `://`, `urllib.request.urlopen(path)` is called on line 213 with the attacker-supplied URL; no URL scheme allowlist, domain whitelist, or network egress control exists.]

Session Fixation via session query parameter in /home — Account takeover: attacker sets a known session ID for the victim, waits for victim to authenticate, then uses the same session ID to access the victim's account. [verified: The `session` query parameter (line 226) is set as the SESSIONID cookie on line 228 with no validation or regeneration; an attacker can pre-set a known session ID for a victim and hijack it after authentication.]

Stored XSS in /profile via CSRF-modified email field — Chained CSRF+XSS attack: attacker changes victim's email to a script payload via CSRF, then when victim views /profile the script executes, enabling full account takeover. [verified: Profile data including the CSRF-modifiable `email` field (user[4]) is rendered via `.format()` on line 263 with no HTML escaping; an attacker can inject script into the email via the CSRF-vulnerable `/settings` endpoint, achieving stored XSS when the victim views `/profile`.]

Hardcoded Backdoor Credentials (dsvpwa/dsvpwa) in login handler — Anyone who discovers or reverse-engineers the application can log in without any valid database account, bypassing all authentication controls. [verified: Line 284 contains hardcoded credentials `username == 'dsvpwa' and password == 'dsvpwa'` that bypass the database authentication entirely; these are embedded in source code and grant immediate access to any discoverer.]
Cross-Site Request Forgery on /settings email update via GET — Attacker can change any authenticated user's email address by tricking them into visiting a malicious page with an or

Cross-Site Request Forgery on /danger account deletion via GET — Attacker can delete any authenticated user's account by luring them to a page with , causing irreversible data loss. [verified: The `/danger` route performs a destructive DELETE via GET (line 366) triggered by the mere presence of `delete` param with no CSRF protection and no X-Frame-Options header; browsers will attach the SESSIONID cookie automatically on cross-origin requests.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read in StaticHandler — Disclosure of sensitive files including the TLS private key (ssl/key.pem), application source code, and system files like /etc/passwd. [verified: StaticHandler.find() does open('./{}'.format(path), 'rb') where path is taken verbatim from self.path (split on '?'); no path normalization or traversal prevention exists — requesting /../ssl/key.pem reads the TLS private key.]

Missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite Cookie Flags — Session cookies can be stolen via XSS (no HttpOnly), intercepted over unencrypted connections (no Secure), and used in CSRF attacks (no SameSite). [verified: Set-Cookie headers in do_GET set only 'path=/'; no Secure (cookies go over plain HTTP), no HttpOnly (accessible to confirmed XSS in the app), and no SameSite (confirmed CSRF endpoints exist) — all three flags are genuinely absent with direct security impact.]

Missing and Misconfigured Security Headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS, XSS Protection) — Weakened browser security allowing clickjacking (no X-Frame-Options), cross-site scripting (disabling XSS auditor, permissive CSP), and MITM downgrade attacks (no HSTS). [verified: X-XSS-Protection:0 explicitly disables browser XSS auditor; CSP default-src * 'unsafe-inline' permits arbitrary origins and inline scripts (no effective restriction); X-Frame-Options is absent on the /danger clickjacking endpoint; HSTS is never set even when --ssl is used — all four misconfigurations have direct impact given the app's demonstrated XSS, CSRF, and clickjacking surfaces.]

Plaintext Password Storage in XML Configuration and SQLite Database — Full compromise of all user credentials if the database or XML file is accessed through path traversal, SQL injection, or filesystem access. [verified: No password hashing exists anywhere in the codebase — passwords are loaded in plaintext from db/users.xml into in-memory SQLite (server.py:15) and compared directly in SQL via string concatenation at attacks.py:289. The SQLite database is reachable via demonstrated SQLi and the XML file via path traversal, making all credentials immediately extractable.]

Open Redirect in /jump via path parameter — Phishing attacks: redirect victims to attacker-controlled sites while appearing to originate from the trusted application domain. [verified: The `path` parameter (line 114) is interpolated directly into `window.location.replace('{path}')` on line 118 with no validation; an attacker can redirect victims to arbitrary external URLs.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint enables credential brute-force — An attacker can brute-force user passwords without any restriction or lockout, gaining unauthorized access to user accounts including the admin account whose credentials are stored in plaintext. [verified: AuthBypass.run() (line 280-297) has no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or incremental delay; the entire server (ThreadingHTTPServer) lacks any rate-limiting middleware, allowing unlimited brute-force attempts.]

User Enumeration via SQL Error-Based Oracle in /login — Attackers can enumerate valid usernames to focus brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks, and confirm which accounts exist in the system. [verified: The `/login` route returns distinct error messages: SQL error on line 290 when injection fails against a valid user vs. generic 'incorrect' message on line 299; this error oracle enables username enumeration.]

Weak Session Token Generation Using Non-Cryptographic PRNG — An attacker can predict session tokens after observing a small number of them, enabling session hijacking for any user. [verified: Session tokens are generated via random.sample (Mersenne Twister, non-cryptographic PRNG) instead of the secrets module; tokens are the sole authentication mechanism, and predictable PRNG state enables session hijacking after observing multiple tokens.]

Sensitive Information Disclosure via Exception Messages in Responses — Attackers gain detailed error information including SQL query structure, file paths, and stack traces that aid in further exploitation. [verified: The outer except Exception as ex: content=str(ex) leaks Python error messages; however, SQL errors cited in the finding are caught internally inside attack handlers (AuthBypass.run, SQLinjection.run) and never reach this outer handler — only file-I/O and format errors propagate here, limiting impact.]
